strengths: Addresses a practically relevant combination of heterogeneous sampling rates, cross-channel dependencies, and missing observations, with a clear forecasting formulation and channel-balanced evaluation metrics.
The architecture is coherent: channel tokens summarize variable numbers of local patches, while structured attention enables cross-channel information exchange and excludes fully missing patches.

Reports consistently better average results across four asynchronous datasets, including an industrial LNG dataset. Table 1 shows CMSE improvements of approximately 1.4–5.3% over the strongest baseline on each dataset.

Provides substantial supplementary evaluation, including five-seed error bars, alternative preprocessing, component and attention-mask ablations, conventional forecasting benchmarks, and additional missingness experiments on ETT1.
weaknesses: The central robustness comparison is confounded. CTF receives explicit missingness masks and random masking augmentation during training, whereas baselines face zero-filled missing blocks without equivalent adaptation. Removing training and inference masking together in the ablation does not separate their effects. Matched augmentation, mask-aware baselines, and stronger imputation-plus-forecasting controls are needed.

The comparison omits methods designed for the target problem. Irregular-time forecasting approaches cited in the paper, including transformable patching graph networks and IMTS-Mixer, are not evaluated; neither is the directly relevant missing-data method SERT. Different fixed sampling periods constitute a structured subset of irregular observations, so the stated distinction does not justify excluding these comparisons.

Training objectives differ materially: Appendix A.2 trains baselines with MSE on interpolated targets, while CTF optimizes channel-aggregated error on observed targets. Although evaluation targets are shared, this does not isolate architectural benefits from the benefit of avoiding artificial training labels. Baselines trained with the same observed-target loss are an essential control.

Several implementation details necessary for reproduction are missing: the dominant-frequency strength threshold, fallback patch-length rule, whether frequencies are estimated per window or once per channel, handling of unseen patch lengths and partially missing patches, and the decoder specification. Dataset split boundaries, normalization, and the industrial dataset's size and availability are also insufficiently documented.

The spectral justification contains technical errors. Appendix B attributes frequency-dependent phase delay to H(f)=sinc²(f), but this real, nonnegative response has zero phase wherever nonzero. Its stated multiplication model also cannot create energy where the input spectrum is zero; explaining interpolation images requires explicitly modeling sampling and reconstruction. Table 6 compares different architectures and therefore does not establish that interpolation causes the forecast differences.

The main SolarWind missingness benchmark deliberately uses patch-sized blocks to exercise CTF's masking mechanism. The additional short-block ETT1 experiment is useful, but robustness to arbitrary block lengths, partial-patch missingness, correlated sensor outages, and missingness on the industrial dataset remains unestablished. Broad real-world robustness claims exceed this evidence.

The methodological novelty is insufficiently distinguished from existing global-token summarization, structured attention, frequency-based patching, and masking augmentation. The combination is plausible, but the missing targeted comparisons and experimental controls prevent a convincing assessment of its incremental value. Parameter-efficiency claims also lack parameter counts or runtime measurements, despite the acknowledged quadratic attention cost.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant combination of heterogeneous channel sampling, cross-channel dependencies, and missing input blocks.
The channel-token architecture offers a coherent way to summarize variable numbers of observed patches and produce channel-specific forecasts without interpolating inputs.

Reports consistently favorable average results across three modified benchmarks and an industrial dataset. Appendices include five-seed variability, forward-fill comparisons, conventional forecasting benchmarks, and useful component and attention-mask ablations.
weaknesses: The central robustness comparison is confounded: CTF receives explicit missingness masks and random masking during training, while baselines face zero-filled test inputs without equivalent adaptations. The patch-masking ablation removes training augmentation and inference masking simultaneously, so it does not isolate their contributions. Matched augmentation, mask-aware baselines, and stronger imputation pipelines are needed.

Baseline coverage misses the most relevant competitors. Despite discussing irregular-time forecasting and missing-data methods, the experiments primarily compare models designed for complete regular grids. Fixed heterogeneous sampling is a structured subset of irregular sampling; comparisons against methods such as the cited transformable patching GNN and IMTS-Mixer are necessary to establish significance.

Appendix A.2 trains baselines on interpolated data with ordinary MSE, whereas CTF optimizes channel-averaged loss on observed targets. Evaluating both on observed targets does not remove this training-objective confound. Baselines should also be trained with the same observed-target loss.

The spectral justification contains technical errors. Appendix B attributes frequency-dependent phase delay to H(f)=sinc²(f), although this real, nonnegative response has zero phase wherever nonzero. Multiplication by this response also cannot create frequencies absent from X(f); a valid discussion of spectral images must explicitly account for sampling. Comparing two different architectures in Table 6 does not establish interpolation as the cause of their forecast differences.

Important implementation and reproduction details are missing: the dominant-frequency strength threshold, fallback patch-length rule, whether FFT-based patch sizes are fixed or recomputed, handling of previously unseen patch lengths, and treatment of partially missing patches. Dataset sizes, chronological split boundaries, and the selected industrial channels are also insufficiently specified.

The missingness evaluation is tailored to the proposed mechanism: SolarWind blocks span exactly one patch length and are described as ensuring fully unobserved patches. The additional short-gap ETT1 results help, but arbitrary block lengths, partial-patch corruption, and genuine industrial missingness remain insufficiently tested.

The architectural novelty is primarily a combination of existing summary tokens, masked attention, frequency-based patching, and patch dropout. Its distinction from related global-token approaches needs sharper evidence. Parameter-efficiency claims lack parameter counts or runtime measurements, and dense quadratic attention is not evaluated at substantial channel counts.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant combination of heterogeneous sampling rates, cross-channel dependencies, and missing input intervals. Channel-level summary tokens provide a coherent way to forecast from variable numbers of observed patches.

Reported results are consistently encouraging across four asynchronous datasets, including an industrial dataset. Table 1 shows improvements over seven forecasting baselines, and the appendix includes five-seed variability estimates and competitive results under conventional sampling.

The ablations investigate channel dependence, patching, masking, channel embeddings, and attention patterns. Additional experiments on input-length variation and alternative preprocessing strengthen the empirical presentation.
weaknesses: The main comparisons omit methods designed for the proposed challenges. Irregular-time forecasting methods such as t-PatchGNN and ContiFormer, and missingness-oriented methods such as SERT, are discussed but not evaluated. Beating conventional forecasters adapted through interpolation does not sufficiently establish competitiveness for asynchronous, partially observed forecasting.

The missingness evaluation confounds architecture with training and information access. CTF receives explicit missingness masks and random masking augmentation, whereas baselines receive zero-filled inputs without comparable adaptations. Removing masking during both training and testing does not separate these effects. Matched augmentation, mask-aware baselines, and stronger imputation-plus-forecasting pipelines are needed.

Training objectives are also unmatched: Appendix A.2 describes baselines trained with MSE on interpolated data, while CTF optimizes channel-aggregated error over actual observations. Although evaluation targets are shared, the results cannot isolate the claimed benefit of avoiding input interpolation from the benefit of avoiding synthetic training targets.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing. These include the threshold for a strong FFT peak, the fallback patch-length rule, whether frequencies are estimated per window or globally, handling of missing observations during FFT estimation, partially missing patches, and previously unseen patch lengths. Dataset sizes, chronological split boundaries, and industrial-data availability are also insufficiently specified.

The interpolation analysis contains technical errors. The stated centered triangular kernel has a real, nonnegative sinc-squared response, so it does not imply the frequency-dependent phase delay claimed in Appendix B. Multiplying a band-limited spectrum by that response cannot create energy outside its support; explaining reconstruction images requires an explicit sampling model. Moreover, comparing two different forecasting architectures does not causally attribute their spectral differences to interpolation.

Real-world robustness is demonstrated narrowly. The main missingness experiment uses SolarWind blocks sized to the model's patches, favoring its whole-patch removal mechanism. Short-block ETT1 experiments help, but missingness robustness is not evaluated on CHS, and the effects of partial patches, correlated sensor outages, and sampling offsets remain unclear.

The architectural novelty is insufficiently distinguished from existing global-token, cross-channel attention, and masking approaches. The paper also provides no runtime, memory, or parameter measurements to substantiate efficiency claims, despite constructing a quadratic attention matrix and evaluating only small channel counts, including just 10 of the 52 industrial channels.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant combination of heterogeneous channel sampling, cross-channel dependence, and missing observations. Channel-token decoding provides a sensible way to accommodate unequal patch counts.

The evaluation covers six datasets, multiple horizons, regular and irregular forecasting baselines, and an industrial application. Reported CMSE improvements include 0.776 versus 0.801 for the strongest baseline on EPA.
Includes useful component and attention-mask ablations, an interpolation-free TimeXer comparison, input-length sensitivity experiments, and per-horizon results with error bars.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons confound architecture with training objectives and augmentation. Appendix A.2 trains regular baselines on interpolated targets using MSE, whereas CTF optimizes channel-aggregated error on observed targets. Comparable missingness augmentation is not established for baselines. ContiFormer is substantially modified by approximating its ODE solver and using regular-baseline preprocessing, without validating fidelity to the original method.

The main missingness benchmark is tailored to CTF: SolarWind missing blocks explicitly span one patch length to ensure fully missing patches. Short-block experiments partially address this limitation, but use restricted baseline sets. The masking ablation simultaneously removes training augmentation and inference masking, preventing attribution of their individual benefits.

Dynamic patching is insufficiently specified and appears dimensionally inconsistent. Appendix A.2 defines the FFT period as Li/k, already measured in channel-specific samples, then divides it again by the sampling factor. The fallback rule, handling of partially missing patches, and management of projection layers when patch lengths change are unclear.

The spectral explanation contains technical errors. The stated centered triangular kernel has a real, nonnegative sinc-squared response and therefore does not imply the claimed frequency-dependent phase delay. Multiplication by that response alone also cannot create energy where the input spectrum is zero; sampling replicas require explicit treatment. Section 6.3 additionally attributes differences between distinct models entirely to interpolation, which the experiment cannot establish.

Reproducibility and dataset consistency need substantial improvement. Exact dataset sizes, chronological splits, and normalization procedures are not specified. Appendix E reports five seeds while the reproducibility statement reports three. EPA includes weekly ozone observations but uses a 96-hour input and shortest prediction window; under the stated floor-based formulation, that channel has zero input and target samples, leaving its loss undefined unless an unreported exception is applied.

Novelty is primarily an integration of existing channel-summary tokens, frequency-based patching, patch dropout, and attention masks. The evidence does not yet establish a sufficiently strong advance over adapted existing models: modified TimeXer outperforms CTF on ETT2, and several other gains are small or tied.

Several claims exceed the results. Table 2 does not show uniformly best CMAE, and masking removal changes CMSE only from 0.452 to 0.458 at missing ratio 0.375. The claimed linear scalability also conflicts with Table 12, where doubling channels from 100 to 200 nearly quadruples runtime and memory; a dense additive attention mask does not itself reduce quadratic computation.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant combination of heterogeneous channel sampling, cross-channel dependencies, and missing observations. Channel-token decoding provides a sensible way to accommodate unequal numbers of input patches.

The evaluation covers six dataset settings, multiple forecasting horizons, regular and irregular forecasting baselines, and additional missingness experiments. Tables 16–17 report variability across repeated runs.

Results show promising forecasting performance, particularly on ETT1 and longer-horizon EPA tasks. The interpolation-free TimeXer comparison and ablations of attention patterns, patching, and channel dependence are useful efforts to isolate contributions.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily an integration of existing channel-summary tokens, frequency-guided patching, patch dropout, and masked attention. The paper acknowledges these precedents, but does not convincingly establish a substantial methodological advance beyond their combination. The strongest architectural comparison is mixed: modified TimeXer outperforms CTF on ETT2 in Table 14.

The main missingness evaluation is tailored to the proposed mechanism. Appendix A.2 specifies SolarWind missing blocks of exactly one patch length, explicitly to enable removal of fully unobserved patches. This does not establish robustness to arbitrary outage lengths, offsets, or partially observed patches. Additional short-block ETT1/EPA experiments help, but comparisons are restricted and CTF loses to Hi-Patch on EPA CMSE at missing ratios 0.2 and 0.3.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently established. CTF receives explicit missingness augmentation during training, without a matched augmentation study for competing models. Regular baselines are described as training on interpolated data with MSE, whereas CTF optimizes observed-target CMSE, leaving the contribution of training-objective differences unresolved. ContiFormer is substantially modified through an unspecified ODE approximation following TimeXer, without validation that this preserves its original capabilities.

The spectral explanation contains technical errors. Appendix B derives a real, nonnegative response H(f) = sinc²(f), which does not imply the claimed frequency-dependent phase delay for centered interpolation. Multiplication by this response also cannot create frequency support absent from X(f); a correct explanation must distinguish sampling replicas from filtering. Section 6.3 additionally attributes performance differences entirely to interpolation despite comparing different architectures.

Dynamic patching is not specified consistently enough to reproduce. Appendix A.2 computes p* = Li/k* from a channel's own sampled sequence, then divides by its sampling factor again; as written, this appears to double-count sampling resolution. The fallback rule, treatment of partial missing patches, and management of projection layers when patch lengths change are insufficiently defined.

Efficiency claims conflict with the implementation description and measurements. Applying a mask to dense attention does not itself avoid computing masked interactions. Table 12 shows runtime increasing from 0.717 to 2.691 seconds and memory from 2844 to 10386 MB when channel count doubles from 100 to 200, contradicting proportional scaling. Appendix G acknowledges quadratic interactions, contrary to the stronger efficiency claims elsewhere.

Reproducibility and reporting need substantial improvement. Dataset sizes, chronological split boundaries, and normalization procedures are not adequately documented; code is deferred until publication. Appendix E states five seeds, while the reproducibility statement states three. Claims of uniformly best performance also overlook counterexamples, including CHS CMAE in Table 1 and SolarWind CMAE at missing ratio 0.375 in Table 2. Together, these issues leave the evidence below the acceptance threshold despite promising empirical results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: forecasting with heterogeneous channel sampling rates, cross-channel dependencies, and missing input blocks.

Channel-token decoding provides a sensible way to accommodate unequal patch counts, and the unified attention mask offers a coherent implementation of temporal aggregation and cross-channel communication.

The evaluation covers multiple datasets, forecasting horizons, and baseline families, with per-horizon error bars and additional missingness experiments. Reported average CMSE improvements are encouraging, particularly on EPA.
The appendix includes useful component and attention-mask ablations, scalability measurements, and an interpolation-free TimeXer adaptation that partially addresses comparison fairness.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness remains unresolved. Appendix A.2 trains regular baselines on interpolated targets with ordinary MSE, whereas CTF optimizes channel-averaged loss over observed targets. Thus, supervision differs alongside architecture. Comparable missingness augmentation for baselines is not established. ContiFormer is substantially modified through an unspecified ODE approximation following TimeXer, without validating fidelity to the original method.

The main robustness experiment closely matches the proposed mechanism: SolarWind missing blocks have exactly one patch length and are constructed to leave whole patches unobserved. Generalization to arbitrary block boundaries, durations, and correlated sensor outages is insufficiently established. Additional short-block experiments help, but handling partially missing patches remains unclear. Disabling training and inference masking simultaneously also prevents isolating their contributions.

Dynamic patching is technically underspecified and appears dimensionally inconsistent. Appendix A.2 defines the FFT period as Li/k, already measured in channel-specific samples, then divides it by the sampling factor again. The fallback rule, treatment of missing values during FFT estimation, and management of projection layers when patch lengths change are not adequately specified.

The spectral justification contains mathematical errors. Under the stated transfer function H(f)=sinc²(f), the centered triangular kernel has zero phase wherever its response is positive; it does not imply the claimed frequency-dependent phase delay. Multiplication by this response also cannot create frequencies absent from X(f) without separately accounting for sampling images. Section 6.3 additionally attributes differences between distinct architectures entirely to interpolation, which the comparison cannot establish.

The contribution primarily combines established channel-summary tokens, frequency-guided patching, patch dropout, and restricted attention. Its incremental value needs stronger controlled evidence: modified TimeXer outperforms CTF on ETT2, several other gains are small, and Table 2 does not support the claim of best CMAE at every missing ratio.

Reproducibility has material gaps. Dataset sizes, chronological splits, and normalization procedures are not concretely documented; code is deferred until publication; and the reproducibility statement reports three seeds while Appendix E reports five. EPA also includes weekly channels despite a 96-hour input and shortest forecast window, yielding zero-length sequences or targets under the stated floor formulas unless an undocumented exception applies.

Efficiency claims overstate the measurements. Structural masking alone does not reduce dense attention complexity, and Table 12 shows approximately quadratic growth at larger channel counts: doubling channels from 100 to 200 increases runtime from 0.717 to 2.691 seconds and memory from 2844 to 10386 MB. These results contradict the proportional-growth narrative.
